subtitle: Transition Year • Applied AI & Digital Skills

blocks.title: AI & Me
blocks.description: Discover where AI appears in everyday life and learn to distinguish AI systems from ordinary software.
blocks.final: Create an AI in My Life summary with three systems, their inputs, outputs, benefits, possible mistakes and one responsible-use question.

sessions.title: Where is AI hiding?
sessions.intro: You probably used AI before school today — even if you never opened a chatbot.
learn: AI can recognise patterns, classify, recommend, predict or generate.
Not every digital tool is AI.
Ask what the system is trying to predict or decide.

activity.title: AI Detective
activity.instructions: Choose the examples that are likely to use AI.

sessions.reflection: Name one digital service you use that may involve AI. What is it trying to predict, classify, recommend or generate?

study.title: What actually makes a system AI?
body: Artificial intelligence describes computer systems that perform tasks such as recognising patterns, making predictions, classifying information, recommending content or generating new text and images.

A useful distinction is between fixed-rule software and learned models. A calculator follows rules written by programmers. A spam filter can learn statistical patterns from examples and estimate whether a new email looks like spam.
Many products combine ordinary software with AI. A maps app can use traditional code to display roads while a model estimates travel time from traffic patterns.
study.example: YouTube can use signals such as what you watched, skipped or liked. A recommendation model estimates which video you may engage with next. That output is a prediction, not a guaranteed fact.

sessions.title: AI Map of My Day
sessions.intro: Move from examples supplied by the course to your own daily life.
learn: AI systems depend on inputs such as clicks, images, text or previous behaviour.
Outputs may be recommendations, rankings, classifications, predictions or generated content.
Useful systems can still make mistakes.

activity.title: Build your AI Day Map
activity.instructions: Add five moments from a typical day. Record the service, likely input and AI output.

sessions.reflection: Which AI system on your map could affect you most if it made a poor decision? Explain why.

study.title: Inputs, models and outputs
body: An AI system receives inputs, processes them with a model and produces an output. Inputs might be text, images, clicks, location context or previous activity.
To understand an AI system, ask: What data goes in? What prediction or decision is made? What happens because of the output?
The same system can create benefits and risks. Navigation can save time but a wrong route can delay you. Recommendation systems can help discovery but may narrow what you repeatedly see.
study.example: Spotify: listening history → recommendation model → suggested playlist. Benefit: music discovery. Limitation: recommendations may become too narrow if the model over-relies on past behaviour.

sessions.title: AI or just software?
sessions.intro: Not every piece of software is AI. Focus on how the behaviour is produced.
learn: Traditional software can follow fixed rules.
Machine-learning systems learn patterns from examples.
One application can contain both approaches.

activity.title: Classify the system
activity.instructions: Choose the best answer for each example.

items.q: A school system calculates attendance percentage using a fixed formula.
A tool predicts which students may need learning support from historical patterns.
A maps app draws roads and predicts journey time using traffic patterns.
A word processor saves a file when you press Save.

sessions.reflection: Write one sentence explaining the difference between a fixed rule and a learned pattern.

study.title: AI versus traditional software
body: Traditional software commonly follows explicit instructions: if a condition occurs, perform a defined action. Machine-learning systems learn patterns from examples and use them on new cases.
The distinction is about how behaviour is produced, not whether the software looks impressive. A timer is useful but usually not AI. A spam predictor is likely using a learned model.
Modern applications often combine both. File saving and user interfaces may be traditional software while recommendations or predictions use AI.
study.example: Attendance percentage = fixed formula. Predicting which students may need extra support from historic patterns = model-based prediction. A school portal could contain both.

sessions.title: Useful, wrong, or unfair?
sessions.intro: AI is not automatically good or bad. Examine consequences and who is affected.
learn: Accuracy matters more when consequences are serious.
Human oversight matters more in high-impact decisions.
Ask who benefits, who could be harmed and how mistakes can be corrected.

activity.title: Impact Meter
activity.instructions: Rate each scenario from Low to High impact.
items: AI recommends a song you dislike.
AI flags a bank payment as possible fraud.
AI suggests which applicant should get a job interview.
AI generates a funny image for a school poster.

sessions.reflection: Should every AI decision require a human to check it? Give one example where oversight matters and one where it may not.

study.title: Impact, error and human oversight
body: AI outputs depend on data, design choices, objectives and context. They are not automatically objective or correct.
The importance of an error depends on consequence. A bad song recommendation is inconvenient; a bad employment or financial decision can have a much larger effect.
Human oversight means a person can review, challenge or override an automated output. It is especially important when decisions significantly affect people.
study.example: A bank fraud flag may need human review because false alarms can block legitimate payments. A wrong music recommendation normally does not need a human reviewer.

blocks.title: Teaching a Machine
blocks.description: Learn how labelled examples train a classifier, then test, evaluate, break and improve the model.
blocks.final: Submit your model evidence: training approach, 10-test log, confusion matrix, one discovered failure, one improvement and a short explanation of why training data affects model behaviour.

sessions.title: You are the classifier
sessions.intro: Before training a machine, notice how humans classify things.
learn: A class is a category the model is asked to recognise.
A feature is a pattern that may help separate classes.
Training examples should represent the situations the model will face.

activity.title: Feature Hunt
activity.instructions: Choose useful clues for distinguishing a cup from a bottle.

sessions.reflection: Which clues could be unreliable? Why?

study.title: How classification works
body: Classification assigns an input to a category called a class. In supervised learning, people provide labelled examples so the model can learn patterns associated with each class.
Features are useful characteristics or patterns. For cups and bottles, shape, handle and proportions may help. Background colour may look useful in training but can be misleading.
A model does not understand objects exactly as a person does. It detects statistical patterns that helped it separate the training examples.
study.example: A model might notice handles, proportions or labels. The challenge is to ensure it learns object-related features rather than accidental background clues.

sessions.title: Train your first model
sessions.intro: Create a simple two-class image classifier using a school-approved visual tool.
learn: Training data are labelled examples used for learning.
Balanced and varied examples improve the chance of generalising.
More nearly identical examples are not automatically better.

activity.title: Train CUP vs BOTTLE
activity.instructions: Follow the steps, then record what you did.
steps: Collect at least 20 examples for each class.
Record what you expect its weakest case will be.

sessions.reflection: What did you change between training examples to make them more varied?

study.title: Training data
body: Training data are labelled examples used by a model to learn. Their quality and coverage strongly influence what the model learns.
A balanced dataset has enough examples of each class. A varied dataset includes realistic differences such as lighting, angle, distance and background.
Repeating nearly identical examples adds less useful information than adding representative variety.
study.example: Twenty cup images from one angle on one desk are less useful than twenty images showing several cups from different angles, distances and backgrounds.

sessions.title: Try to break it
sessions.intro: A strong tester searches for failure instead of only showing that a model works.
learn: Test data should include unseen examples.
Accuracy is the share of predictions that were correct.
Errors reveal where a model may not generalise.

activity.title: Model Test Lab
activity.instructions: Run at least 10 tests and record actual class, prediction and notes.

sessions.reflection: Which type of test failed most often? What changed compared with the training data?

study.title: Testing and generalisation
body: Testing asks whether a model works on examples it did not simply memorise during training. Useful tests include variation and difficult cases.
Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total tests. It is useful but does not explain which kinds of mistakes occurred.
Generalisation means performing well on new, realistic examples rather than only the training set.
study.example: If a classifier gets 8 of 10 unseen examples correct, accuracy is 80%. Investigate the two failures instead of stopping at the percentage.

sessions.title: Read the confusion matrix
sessions.intro: A single accuracy number can hide the kinds of mistakes a model makes.
learn: A confusion matrix compares actual and predicted labels.
Correct predictions sit on the main diagonal.
Different error types can have different consequences.

activity.title: Build the matrix
activity.instructions: Enter your Cup→Cup, Cup→Bottle, Bottle→Cup and Bottle→Bottle counts.

sessions.reflection: If overall accuracy is high, can the model still have an important weakness? Explain.

study.title: Confusion matrices
body: A confusion matrix separates correct predictions from different types of error. Rows represent what the example actually was and columns represent what the model predicted.
For two classes there are four cells. The two matching cells are correct predictions; the off-diagonal cells are mistakes.
Two models can have the same accuracy but fail in different ways, so error types matter.
study.example: Cup→Cup=4, Cup→Bottle=1, Bottle→Cup=2, Bottle→Bottle=3 gives 7 correct out of 10, or 70% accuracy.

sessions.title: Shortcut learning & bias
sessions.intro: Models may learn patterns we never intended them to learn.
learn: Shortcut learning uses an easy correlated feature instead of the intended concept.
Unrepresentative data can create systematic performance gaps.
Testing across varied conditions helps reveal weaknesses.

activity.title: The Background Trap
activity.q: Every cup training image used a white desk and every bottle a dark desk. A cup on a dark desk is predicted as Bottle. Why?
options: The model may have learned background colour as a shortcut.
Dark desks change cups into bottles.

sessions.reflection: Give another example of an accidental shortcut an image model might learn.

study.title: Shortcut learning and bias
body: A model searches for statistical patterns that reduce error. It does not automatically know which pattern humans intended it to learn.
Shortcut learning occurs when a model relies on an easy correlated signal instead of the real concept. Performance can collapse when the environment changes.
Bias can appear when training data do not represent relevant groups or conditions well. Varied testing helps expose these gaps.
study.example: If cup photos always use a white desk and bottle photos a dark desk, the model may learn desk colour. A cup on a dark desk can then be misclassified.

sessions.title: Improve, retrain, compare
sessions.intro: Iteration is part of machine learning. Improve the data, then compare evidence.
learn: Change the dataset based on observed failures.
Retest with similar challenge cases so comparison is meaningful.
A better model is supported by evidence, not confidence.

activity.title: Model Improvement Plan
activity.instructions: Select at least three improvements and record the before/after result.
items: Repeat exactly the same photo many times

sessions.reflection: What change made the biggest improvement, or what would you test next?

study.title: Improving a model with evidence
body: Machine learning is iterative: train, test, diagnose failures, improve the data or design, then retest.
A fair comparison keeps the test challenge as similar as possible before and after the change.
Good improvement decisions are evidence-based: identify a failure pattern, make a targeted change and measure the result.
study.example: If dark backgrounds cause cup errors, add cups and bottles on both light and dark backgrounds, retrain, then repeat the same background tests.
